claim: TALENs were used to stably introduce a doxycycline-inducible NGN2 cassette into the AAVS1 safe harbor locus of the hPSC line H1.
source: To overcome the limitations of lentiviral titer used to transduce NGN2 and to enhance differentiation efficiency, we used a pair of TALENs to stably introduce a doxycycline-inducible NGN2 cassette (Zhang et al., 2013) into the AAVS1 safe harbor locus of the hPSC line H1 to generate a zeocin-resistant doxycycline-inducible NGN2 hPSC line, referred to as iNGN2-hPSC (Figure 1a), similar to the approach used by Meijer et al., 2019.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure used to generate the cell line, with reference to Figure 1a showing the schematic.

claim: The iNGN2-hPSC line has a normal karyotype 46,XY.
source: Upon transfection, cells were selected for geneticin resistance and individual clones were isolated, expanded, re-plated for genomic DNA extraction and PCR analysis of the transgene integration, and further analyzed by G-band karyotyping (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows cytogenetic analysis demonstrating an apparently normal karyotype 46,XY.

claim: hNs begin to show electrophysiological activity around day 21 in vitro displaying spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents (sEPSCs) and NMDAR-mediated currents.
source: Data from our laboratory and others confirm that hNs begin to show electrophysiological activity around day 21 in vitro displaying spontaneous excitatory post-synaptic currents (sEPSCs) and NMDAR-mediated currents (Meijer et al., 2019; Nehme et al., 2018; Susco et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies from the authors' laboratory and others.

claim: At day 21 in vitro, synapses and synaptic network are still maturing in hNs.
source: However, it is important to note that at this timepoint synapses and synaptic network are still maturing.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the developmental stage of the neurons at the timepoint studied.

claim: The platform quantifies presynaptic puncta defined as SYNAPSIN1 puncta assembled on MAP2-expressing neuronal dendrites.
source: We then quantified presynaptic puncta, defined as SYNAPSIN1 puncta assembled on MAP2-expressing neuronal dendrites, which are (1) robustly captured in our human cellular models; (2) essential for normal neuronal development with perturbations implicated in disease (Südhof, 2017; Waites and Garner, 2011); (3) a prerequisite for the assembly of postsynaptic machinery (Friedman et al., 2000; Rohrbough et al., 2007; Sanes and Lichtman, 2001); and (4) successfully measured in multiple synaptic screens performed in mouse (Hempel et al., 2011; Spicer et al., 2018), as well as in small-scale synaptic measurements performed using human cellular systems (Chanda et al., 2019; Pak et al., 2015; Yi et al., 2016).
evidence: The definition is provided with supporting citations for the biological relevance and prior use of these markers.

claim: SYNAPSIN1 appeared in a discrete punctate staining pattern localized on and along the clearly defined MAP2-expressing neurites.
source: SYNAPSIN1 appeared in a discrete punctate staining pattern localized on and along the clearly defined MAP2-expressing neurites (Figure 1d).
evidence: This observation is supported by the immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Roughly half of the SYNAPSIN1 signal on MAP2 colocalized with synaptophysin and vice versa.
source: Roughly half of the SYNAPSIN1 signal on MAP2 colocalized with synaptophysin and vice versa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrates the colocalization percentage.

claim: Of the PSD-95 puncta on MAP2, 43.1% also colocalized with SYNAPSIN1 and of the SYNAPSIN1 puncta on MAP2, 28.8% colocalized with PSD-95.
source: We observed moderate colocalization of PSD-95 with SYNAPSIN1; of the PSD-95 puncta on MAP2, 43.1% also colocalized with SYNAPSIN1 and of the SYNAPSIN1 puncta on MAP2, 28.8% colocalized with PSD-95 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrates the colocalization percentages.

claim: The partial overlap between SYNAPSIN1 and synaptophysin may indicate that SYNAPSIN1 expression occurs prior to synaptophysin, potentially reflecting maturation of vesicle exocytosis mechanisms prior to endocytosis mechanisms.
source: Interestingly, studies in rodent cortex report that SYNAPSIN1 expression occurs prior to synaptophysin, potentially reflecting maturation of vesicle exocytosis mechanisms prior to endocytosis mechanisms (Pinto et al., 2013), which may contribute to the partial overlap in our assay.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to a previous study in rodent cortex.

claim: SYNAPSIN1 is a more robust and specific marker for presynaptic terminals than synaptophysin, with reports of synaptophysin also expressed at extrasynaptic sites.
source: In general, SYNAPSIN1 is reported to be a more robust and specific marker for presynaptic terminals, with reports of synaptophysin also expressed at extrasynaptic sites (Micheva et al., 2010; Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies comparing these markers.

claim: The signal obtained for synaptophysin was weak compared with the signal obtained for SYNAPSIN1.
source: Indeed, the signal we obtained for synaptophysin was weak compared with the signal we obtained for SYNAPSIN1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by the images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The moderate colocalization of PSD-95 with SYNAPSIN1 may indicate presynaptic assembly occurring prior to postsynaptic assembly at this early stage of neuronal development.
source: This may indicate presynaptic assembly occurring prior to postsynaptic assembly (Friedman et al., 2000; Rohrbough et al., 2007; Sanes and Lichtman, 2001) at this early stage of neuronal development.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous studies on synapse development.

claim: The signal obtained for PSD-95 was weak and of insufficient quality as well as consistency for screening applications.
source: Again, at this developmental timepoint, the signal obtained for PSD-95 was weak and of insufficient quality as well as consistency for screening applications (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is supported by the images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4000 surviving hNs per well was a minimum to establish a synaptic network and 12,000 surviving hNs per well was the maximum to circumvent hN clumping and reliably discriminate distinct SYNAPSIN1 puncta.
source: Of note, while several synaptic screens using mouse primary neurons report plating a range of 10,000–20,000 neurons per well in 96-well plates (Nieland et al., 2014; Sharma et al., 2012), we validated the number of hNs from a randomly selected plate 1 d after co-culture and found that 4000 surviving hNs per well was a minimum to establish a synaptic network and 12,000 surviving hNs per well was the maximum to circumvent hN clumping as well as reliably discriminate distinct SYNAPSIN1 puncta and track MAP2-expressing neurites for image processing (Figure 1e).
evidence: This threshold was validated through experimental testing shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Consistency of plating was high within batches, with an 8% covariance threshold.
source: Importantly, consistency of plating was high within batches, with an 8% covariance threshold (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Incubating human co-cultures with SYN1 targeting siRNA for 72 hr significantly reduced presynaptic density compared to GAPD and non-targeting siRNA controls.
source: Although siRNA-mediated knockdown is heterogeneous, incubating human co-cultures with SYN1 targeting siRNA for 72 hr significantly reduced presynaptic density compared to GAPD and non-targeting siRNA controls, with no or minimal impact on the area covered by MAP2-positive neurites or the total number of DAPI-positive neurites in any condition (Figure 1g; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: SYNAPSIN1 puncta with diameters between 1 and 6 pixels were selected based on analyses of their cumulative distribution.
source: SYNAPSIN1 puncta with diameters between 1 and 6 pixels were selected based on analyses of their cumulative distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), a setting which can be customized in our platform.
evidence: This selection criterion is based on the cumulative distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: 92.94% of the control and treated wells had a Z-score for synaptic density between –2 and +2.
source: Importantly, 92.94% of the control and treated wells had a Z-score for synaptic density between –2 and +2, underscoring the reliability and robustness of our automated high-content synaptic screening platform (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statistic is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and demonstrates the platform's reliability.

claim: Thirteen small molecules (3.46% of the library) did not meet the quality control requirements.
source: Thirteen small molecules (3.46% of the library) did not meet the above quality control requirements and seven (1.86% of the library) reduced the density of SYNAPSIN1 puncta on MAP2 neurites by a Z-score ≤–3 and reduced the area covered by MAP2-positive neurites by a Z-score ≤ –2 (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is reported from the primary screen results shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Seven small molecules (1.86% of the library) reduced the density of SYNAPSIN1 puncta on MAP2 neurites by a Z-score ≤–3 and reduced the area covered by MAP2-positive neurites by a Z-score ≤ –2.
source: Thirteen small molecules (3.46% of the library) did not meet the above quality control requirements and seven (1.86% of the library) reduced the density of SYNAPSIN1 puncta on MAP2 neurites by a Z-score ≤–3 and reduced the area covered by MAP2-positive neurites by a Z-score ≤ –2 (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is reported from the primary screen results shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The seven small molecules that reduced synaptic density and MAP2 coverage were known to induce apoptosis or catalytic process of autophagy.
source: as expected, these small molecules were known to induce apoptosis or catalytic process of autophagy (Boccadoro et al., 2005; Piva et al., 2008; Reddy et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on these small molecules.

claim: Six out of 17 small molecules tested exhibited a significant dose-dependent increase in presynaptic density compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: We found that 6 out of 17 small molecules tested exhibited a significant dose-dependent increase in presynaptic density compared to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: All three BET inhibitors ((+)-JQ1, Birabresib, and I-BET151) increased presynaptic density with similar magnitudes of effect.
source: Notably, all three BET inhibitors ((+)-JQ1, Birabresib, and I-BET151) increased presynaptic density with similar magnitudes of effect (Figure 3b and c and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data shown in Figure 3b, 3c and supplementary figures.

claim: ROCK1/ROCK2 inhibition through GSK429286A can enhance synapse formation in human neurons.
source: BI-D1870 and GSK429286A also elicited a significant dose–response, indicating that the synaptic connectivity in hNs is modulated through multiple intracellular pathways (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2). Indeed, previous studies have shown that ROCK1/ROCK2 inhibition can enhance synapse formation in rodent models (Swanger et al., 2015), consistent with our results from GSK429286A treatment of hN + hpA co-cultures.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data and supported by citation to a previous rodent study.

claim: VS-5584, an ATP-competitive Pi3K inhibitor with equivalent potency against all human isoforms (α, β, γ, and δ), drove a concentration-dependent increase in presynaptic density compared to the DMSO-treated wells, but not TG100-15, a selective inhibitor of the γ and δ isoforms.
source: Finally, VS-5584, an ATP-competitive Pi3K inhibitor with equivalent potency against all human isoforms (α, β, γ, and δ), drove a concentration-dependent increase in presynaptic density compared to the DMSO-treated wells, but not TG100-15, a selective inhibitor of the γ and δ isoforms (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the preferential immune-cell expression of Pi3Kγ and δ versus the ubiquitous expression patterns of Pi3Kα and β (Winkler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, with interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The six validated small molecules showed minimal to no toxicity or effect on neurite outgrowth at lower doses.
source: The six validated small molecules showed minimal to no toxicity or effect on neurite outgrowth at lower doses, as assessed by the number of DAPI-positive nuclei detected and the area covered by MAP2-positive neurites (Figure 3b–d and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3b-d and supplementary figures.

claim: Four out of six small molecules, including all three BET inhibitors, increased presynaptic density in hN + hpA co-cultures derived from an independent hPSC line.
source: We then derived hNs from an independent hPSC line with the same stable, inducible AAVS1 NGN2 integration strategy described above, and confirmed that four out of six small molecules, including all three BET inhibitors, increased presynaptic density in hN + hpA co-cultures at these specific concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), further validating our previous findings and indicating that the effects of the selected small molecules were generally reproducible across cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the validation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: None of the six small molecules elicited a significant increase in presynaptic density in hN monocultures.
source: While hN monocultures passed all quality control and thresholding criteria (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), none of the six small molecules elicited a significant increase in presynaptic density in this condition (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Small molecule treatment did not significantly affect the level of SYNAPSIN1 protein expression in either the hN monoculture or hN + hpA co-culture conditions.
source: Small molecule treatment also did not significantly affect the level of SYNAPSIN1 protein expression in either the hN monoculture or hN + hpA co-culture conditions as assessed by western blot analysis (Figure 4e and f), indicating that the differences observed between hN monocultures and hN + hpA co-cultures after small molecule addition were more likely due to changes in SYNAPSIN1 protein localization as opposed to overall protein abundance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the western blot data shown in Figure 4e and 4f.

claim: The addition of hpAs had a significant effect on synapse development in the absence of small molecules, including a significant increase in SYNAPSIN1 presynaptic density as well as in the size of individual SYNAPSIN1 puncta with a modest reduction in the area covered by MAP2-positive neurites.
source: The addition of hpAs also had a significant effect on synapse development in the absence of small molecules, including a significant increase in SYNAPSIN1 presynaptic density as well as in the size of individual SYNAPSIN1 puncta with a modest reduction in the area covered by MAP2-positive neurites (Figure 5a–e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison data shown in Figure 5a-e.

claim: The addition of hpAs roughly doubled both the density and size of SYNAPSIN1 puncta on MAP2-positive neurites compared with hNs alone.
source: Indeed, the addition of hpAs roughly doubled both the density and size of SYNAPSIN1 puncta on MAP2-positive neurites compared with hNs alone (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantification shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claim: hNs can form quantifiable presynaptic puncta that can be reliably captured by the platform in the absence of astrocytes.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that hNs can form quantifiable presynaptic puncta that can be reliably captured by our platform in the absence of astrocytes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results with hN monocultures.

claim: hpAs contributed to the assembly or localization of presynaptic machinery.
source: However, hpAs contributed to the assembly or localization of presynaptic machinery, underscoring the relevance of astrocytes in human synaptic screening applications.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of hN monocultures versus hN + hpA co-cultures.

claim: Both (+)-JQ1 and I-BET151 had very large effect sizes in the primary screen, with a Cohen's d of 2.914 for (+)-JQ1 and 3.710 for I-BET151.
source: Notably, both (+)-JQ1 and I-BET151 had very large effect sizes in the primary screen, with a Cohen's d of 2.914 for (+)-JQ1 and 3.710 for I-BET151 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is reported from the power calculation analysis shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: In order to achieve 95% power (one-sided) to detect small effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.2), experiments would require around n = 270 replicates, while medium effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.5) would require around n = 43 replicates, and large effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.8) would require around n = 17 replicates.
source: Overall, in order to achieve 95% power (one-sided) to detect small effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.2), experiments would require around n = 270 replicates, while medium effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.5) would require around n = 43 replicates, and large effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.8) would require around n = 17 replicates.
evidence: This is reported from the power calculation analysis.

claim: Applying an adjusted p-value cut-off of 0.05 and log2 fold change cut-offs of ≤–1 and ≥ 1, a comparable number of significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified after (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment compared to DMSO control.
source: Applying an adjusted p-value cut-off of 0.05 and log2 fold change cut-offs of ≤–1 and ≥ 1, we identified a comparable number of significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) after (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment compared to DMSO control (Figure 6b and c, Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the volcano plots shown in Figure 6b and 6c and the supplementary data files.

claim: A majority of DEGs were downregulated after BET inhibition.
source: A majority of DEGs were downregulated after BET inhibition (Figure 6b and c), consistent with the known roles of BET proteins in transcriptional activation, and were also shared between the (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment conditions (n = 2368; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the volcano plots in Figure 6b and 6c and the Venn diagram in Figure 6d.

claim: 2368 DEGs were shared between the (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment conditions.
source: A majority of DEGs were downregulated after BET inhibition (Figure 6b and c), consistent with the known roles of BET proteins in transcriptional activation, and were also shared between the (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment conditions (n = 2368; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 6d.

claim: Strong positive correlation in the magnitudes of effect of (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment was observed with a Pearson's r score of 0.9404.
source: We also observed strong positive correlation in the magnitudes of effect of (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment as attested by the Pearson's r score of 0.9404 (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the scatterplot shown in Figure 6e.

claim: BRD4 (p=1.61 × 10–17), (+)-JQ1 (p=0.000206), and Birabresib (p=4.59 × 10–18) were all strongly predicted to be upstream regulators of the shared DEGs.
source: Using ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA), we confirmed that BRD4 (p=1.61 × 10–17), (+)-JQ1 (p=0.000206), and Birabresib (p=4.59 × 10–18) were all strongly predicted to be upstream regulators of the shared DEGs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the IPA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Signaling pathways such as 'DNA methylation and transcriptional repression' and 'axonal guidance' were enriched in the upregulated DEGs.
source: Signaling pathways such as 'DNA methylation and transcriptional repression' and 'axonal guidance' were enriched in the upregulated DEGs, while signaling pathways such as 'wound healing' and 'neuroinflammation' enriched in the downregulated DEGs (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Signaling pathways such as 'wound healing' and 'neuroinflammation' were enriched in the downregulated DEGs.
source: Signaling pathways such as 'DNA methylation and transcriptional repression' and 'axonal guidance' were enriched in the upregulated DEGs, while signaling pathways such as 'wound healing' and 'neuroinflammation' enriched in the downregulated DEGs (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Significant enrichment was found for the terms 'integral component of postsynaptic membrane' and 'postsynaptic membrane' with modest but significant enrichment for additional presynaptic terms.
source: We found significant enrichment for the terms 'integral component of postsynaptic membrane' and 'postsynaptic membrane' with modest but significant enrichment for additional presynaptic terms (Figure 6g and h, Supplementary file 5) consistent with a role for BET proteins in the regulation of pre- and postsynaptic genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SynGO analysis shown in Figure 6g and 6h.

claim: Examples of individual pre- and postsynaptic genes upregulated following BET inhibition include the presynaptic cell adhesion molecule Neurexin 3 (NRXN3), the synaptic vesicle gene Amphiphysin (AMPH), the transmembrane Eph receptor ligand Ephrin-B2 (EFNB2) involved in AMPAR stabilization, and the postsynaptic scaffolding factors BAR/IMD Domain Containing Adaptor Protein 2 (BAIAP2) and Homer Scaffold Protein 1 (HOMER1).
source: Examples of individual pre- and postsynaptic genes upregulated following BET inhibition include the presynaptic cell adhesion molecule Neurexin 3 (NRXN3), the synaptic vesicle gene Amphiphysin (AMPH), the transmembrane Eph receptor ligand Ephrin-B2 (EFNB2) involved in AMPAR stabilization, and the postsynaptic scaffolding factors BAR/IMD Domain Containing Adaptor Protein 2 (BAIAP2) and Homer Scaffold Protein 1 (HOMER1) (Figure 6i).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment each roughly doubled the expression of pre- and postsynaptic genes.
source: Indeed, (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment each roughly doubled the expression of these pre- and postsynaptic genes.
evidence: This is based on the gene expression data shown in Figure 6i.

claim: Both (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib significantly increased protein expression levels of the postsynaptic scaffolding factors BAIAP2 and Homer1 compared with DMSO-treated control.
source: Additionally, western blot analysis revealed that both (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib significantly increased protein expression levels of the postsynaptic scaffolding factors BAIAP2 and Homer1 compared with DMSO-treated control (Figure 6j), paralleling the transcript-level changes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the western blot data shown in Figure 6j.

claim: BET inhibition led to upregulation of the anti-inflammatory factor Interleukin 11 (IL11).
source: Consistent with the pathway analyses, we also observed modulation of the expression of several astrocyte-secreted factors including upregulation of the anti-inflammatory factor Interleukin 11 (IL11), downregulation of the pro-inflammatory factor Interleukin 6 (IL6), and downregulation of the synapse disassembly factor Secreted Protein Acidic And Cysteine Rich (SPARC) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: BET inhibition led to downregulation of the pro-inflammatory factor Interleukin 6 (IL6).
source: Consistent with the pathway analyses, we also observed modulation of the expression of several astrocyte-secreted factors including upregulation of the anti-inflammatory factor Interleukin 11 (IL11), downregulation of the pro-inflammatory factor Interleukin 6 (IL6), and downregulation of the synapse disassembly factor Secreted Protein Acidic And Cysteine Rich (SPARC) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: BET inhibition led to downregulation of the synapse disassembly factor Secreted Protein Acidic And Cysteine Rich (SPARC).
source: Consistent with the pathway analyses, we also observed modulation of the expression of several astrocyte-secreted factors including upregulation of the anti-inflammatory factor Interleukin 11 (IL11), downregulation of the pro-inflammatory factor Interleukin 6 (IL6), and downregulation of the synapse disassembly factor Secreted Protein Acidic And Cysteine Rich (SPARC) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: BET inhibition led to downregulation of Caspase 1 (CASP1) and Gasdermin D (GSDMD).
source: Combined with downregulation of Caspase 1 (CASP1) and Gasdermin D (GSDMD) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), these results point to a general anti-inflammatory response following BET inhibition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: CASP1, GSDMD, and IL6 have all previously been shown to be downregulated by (+)-JQ1 treatment, consistent with the known role of BET proteins in promotion of the inflammatory response.
source: Indeed, CASP1, GSDMD, and IL6 have all previously been shown to be downregulated by (+)-JQ1 treatment, consistent with the known role of BET proteins in promotion of the inflammatory response (Wang et al., 2021b; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in gene transcription were highly concordant between both (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment conditions, with similar magnitudes of effect.
source: Importantly, changes in gene transcription were again highly concordant between both (+)-JQ1 and Birabresib treatment conditions, with similar magnitudes of effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the gene expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: BET inhibition can lead to upregulation of synaptic genes.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that BET inhibition can lead to upregulation of synaptic genes, consistent with our screening results showing an increase in presynaptic density and supporting a role for BET proteins in synapse assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcriptional analysis results.

claim: The transcriptional results support the robustness of the platform for detecting human synaptic modulators in vitro.
source: These results also support the robustness of our platform for detecting human synaptic modulators in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the concordance between screening and transcriptional results.

claim: BET protein expression is downregulated throughout neuronal differentiation, with knockdown of BET proteins sufficient to enhance differentiation.
source: Indeed, BET protein expression is downregulated throughout neuronal differentiation, with knockdown of BET proteins sufficient to enhance differentiation (Li et al., 2016) consistent with a role for BET proteins in negatively regulating neuronal development.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The results from BET inhibition in human cellular models contrast with a subset of data generated in adult mouse brain.
source: These results contrast with a subset of data generated in adult mouse brain and are thus likely to be dependent upon factors such as brain cell type, developmental stage, and timing of drug treatment.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies in rodent models mentioned earlier in the manuscript.

claim: BET inhibitors are currently in use in clinical trials for cancer and are proposed for the treatment of developmental as well as degenerative diseases.
source: Resolving potential neurological benefits and/or consequences of BET inhibition in different contexts including in diverse brain cell types and developmental stages is essential as these drugs are currently in use in clinical trials for cancer and are proposed for the treatment of developmental as well as degenerative diseases (Korb et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The platform is the first automated and quantitative high-content synaptic phenotyping platform for human neurons and astrocytes.
source: Specifically: (1) we generated the first automated and quantitative high-content synaptic phenotyping platform for human neurons and astrocytes, which can now be leveraged for study of basic human synaptic mechanisms, dissection of complex human disease and drug discovery efforts
evidence: This is stated as a key advance of the study.

claim: The stable NGN2 integration strategy for scaled generation of hNs from hPSCs is well suited for screening applications.
source: (2) our results demonstrate that the stable NGN2 integration strategy for scaled generation of hNs from hPSCs is well suited for screening applications
evidence: This is stated as a key advance of the study based on the experimental results.

claim: The platform is compatible with both small molecule as well as siRNA-based manipulations.
source: (3) our platform is compatible with both small molecule as well as siRNA-based manipulations
evidence: This is stated as a key advance of the study and demonstrated by the experimental results.

claim: The platform captures key parameters of human synaptic connectivity including the number and the area of individual presynaptic contacts as well as the coverage of MAP2-positive neurites and overall cell viability.
source: (4) our platform captures key parameters of human synaptic connectivity including the number and the area of individual presynaptic contacts as well as the coverage of MAP2-positive neurites and overall cell viability
evidence: This is stated as a key advance of the study and demonstrated by the experimental results.

claim: The analyses underscore the relevance of astrocytes when studying human synaptic mechanisms and drug response.
source: (5) while compatible with analyses of hN monocultures, our analyses underscore the relevance of astrocytes when studying human synaptic mechanisms and drug response
evidence: This is stated as a key advance of the study based on the experimental results comparing monocultures and co-cultures.

claim: Different human genetic backgrounds can be employed in the platform to dissect disease mechanisms.
source: and (6) different human genetic backgrounds can be employed in our platform to dissect disease mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a key advance of the study and demonstrated by testing in multiple cell lines.

claim: The platform was specifically designed for use with human neurons and astrocytes and alterations to the neuronal differentiation paradigms or species, or the addition of other brain cell types may require modest customization steps.
source: There are also several limitations to our approach: (1) our platform was specifically designed for use with human neurons and astrocytes and alterations to the neuronal differentiation paradigms or species, or the addition of other brain cell types may require modest customization steps
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: The platform is based on high-content imaging, and neurophysiological function must be assessed using separate methodology, likely at lower throughput.
source: (2) our platform is based on high-content imaging, and neurophysiological function must be assessed using separate methodology, likely at lower throughput
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Reliance on SYNAPSIN1 on MAP2 as a readout for presynaptic density in developing neurons may be capturing sites that do not then develop into fully functional/mature synapses with postsynaptic partners.
source: (3) similarly, reliance on SYNAPSIN1 on MAP2 as a readout for presynaptic density in developing neurons may be capturing sites that do not then develop into fully functional/mature synapses with postsynaptic partners
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: While the timepoints of manipulations and analyses can be altered in the assay, longitudinal studies in the same cells are not possible unless suitable genetically encoded fluorescent markers are employed.
source: (4) while the timepoints of manipulations and analyses can be altered in our assay, longitudinal studies in the same cells are not possible unless suitable genetically encoded fluorescent markers are employed
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: The platform is designed for 2D culture to allow for precise control over cell densities and ratios but does not fully reflect the structural complexity present in 3D systems.
source: and (5) our platform is designed for 2D culture to allow for precise control over cell densities and ratios but does not fully reflect the structural complexity present in 3D systems (e.g., spheroids, organoids).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Species-divergent features of brain cell types have been increasingly identified.
source: Based upon increasing evidence of species-divergent features of brain cell types, coupled with emerging studies of complex human disease genetics, we developed the first automated and quantitative high-content synaptic phenotyping platform using human neurons and astrocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as motivation for the study.

claim: The platform screened the effects of 376 small molecules on presynaptic density, neurite outgrowth, and cell viability.
source: To establish the robustness of our platform, we screened the effects of 376 small molecules on presynaptic density, neurite outgrowth, and cell viability, validating six small molecules that specifically enhanced human presynaptic density in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the experimental approach.

claim: Six small molecules were validated that specifically enhanced human presynaptic density in vitro.
source: To establish the robustness of our platform, we screened the effects of 376 small molecules on presynaptic density, neurite outgrowth, and cell viability, validating six small molecules that specifically enhanced human presynaptic density in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.
